title: Audit Strategy, Audit Planning and Audit Programme
outcomes: Explain the need for and benefits of audit planning under SA 300.
Describe preliminary engagement activities and planning activities.
Distinguish the overall audit strategy from the audit plan and explain their documentation and revision.
Explain the audit programme, its construction, evidence it targets, and its merits and demerits.

meta.exam_tip: Case MCQs ask you to classify activities as preliminary, strategy or plan; theory asks benefits of planning, strategy vs plan, and audit programme merits.

concepts.title: Why plan an audit (SA 300)
body: SA 300 requires the auditor to plan the audit so that it is performed effectively.

Adequate planning helps the auditor (table): focus on important areas, spot and solve problems early, organise the engagement efficiently, select a team with the right skills, direct, supervise and review team members, and co-ordinate the work of experts and other auditors.
Good planning keeps audit risk — the risk of giving an inappropriate opinion — at an acceptably low level.
concepts.analogy: Planning an audit is like planning a wedding: guest list (scope), budget (resources), schedule (timing) and who handles what (team) — skip it and something important is forgotten.
concepts.work: Audit firms hold planning meetings weeks before year-end to allocate staff and fix inventory-count dates.

head: Benefit of planning
What it means in practice
rows: Attention to important areas
More time and senior staff on high-risk balances
Early identification of problems
Issues such as missing records surface before the deadline
Efficient organisation
Work is sequenced and budgeted, avoiding last-minute rush
Right team for the risks
Experienced members and specialists where needed
Direction, supervision and review
Clear assignment makes reviewing work easier
Co-ordination with others
Work of experts and other auditors is lined up in time
blocks.title: Benefits of planning

concepts.title: Planning is continuous and iterative
body: Planning is not a single phase; it is a continuous, iterative process that often starts soon after the previous audit ends and runs until the current one is completed.

Before identifying risks, planning considers matters such as analytical procedures as risk assessment, understanding the legal and regulatory framework (e.g. RBI rules for banks, TRAI rules for telecom companies), materiality, the need for experts and other risk assessment procedures.
The engagement partner and key team members take part in planning, bringing experience and insight.
The auditor may discuss parts of the plan with management to ease the audit, but must not reveal so much that the audit becomes predictable and less effective.
concepts.analogy: Planning is like a GPS route — set at the start but recalculated whenever the road ahead changes.
concepts.work: Auditors often begin next year's planning while writing this year's management letter.

concepts.title: Preliminary engagement activities
body: Before planning proper, the auditor performs preliminary engagement activities.

(A) Acceptance and continuance procedures: consider the integrity of owners and key management, the team's competence, and issues from current and earlier audits; for a new client, communicate with the previous auditor.

(B) Ethical requirements and independence: the engagement partner stays alert for breaches, identifies threats to independence, applies safeguards or withdraws where permitted, and reports unresolved matters to the firm.
(C) Terms of engagement: an engagement letter sent before the audit begins avoids misunderstandings.
These steps reveal events or conditions that could affect the auditor's ability to plan and perform the audit.
concepts.analogy: Before starting a journey with someone, you check whether you trust them, whether you are fit to travel, and agree who pays for what.
concepts.work: Firms run a formal acceptance checklist (with background checks on promoters) before taking a new listed client.

concepts.title: Overall audit strategy
body: The overall audit strategy decides the audit's scope, its timing and its direction, and guides the detailed plan.

It helps decide: which resources to use for specific areas (experienced staff on high-risk areas, experts for complex matters); how much to allocate (team size at inventory counts, review of other auditors in group audits, budget hours); when to deploy them (interim stage or key cut-off dates); and how to manage, direct and supervise them (briefings, reviews, quality reviews).

Factors considered: (a) characteristics defining scope — reporting framework, business segments needing special knowledge, industry reporting rules, use of earlier audit evidence; (b) reporting objectives — the entity's reporting timetable, meetings with management, expected reports and communications; (c) significant factors directing the team — materiality, high-risk areas, volume of transactions, industry and legal changes; (d) results of preliminary activities and knowledge from other engagements; (e) nature, timing and extent of resources needed.
concepts.analogy: Strategy is the captain's match plan: who bowls at the death, which fielder guards the boundary, and when to take the powerplay.
concepts.work: For a company with plants in five states, the strategy decides which plants senior staff visit at year-end.

concepts.title: The audit plan and its link with strategy
body: The audit plan, developed after the strategy, describes: (i) which risk assessment procedures will be done, when and how much; (ii) the same three aspects for further audit procedures at the assertion level; and (iii) any other procedures the SAs require.
Knowledge of the client's business is essential to develop a sound plan.
Risk assessment procedures are planned early; further procedures depend on their results, and some may start before all others are planned.
Strategy and plan are closely inter-related, not strictly sequential — a change in one may require a change in the other. Both remain the auditor's responsibility.
concepts.analogy: If strategy says "attack the opponent's weak bowler", the plan says which batsman faces him, in which over and with what shots.
concepts.work: A plan may specify, for example, confirmation of the top 20 debtors as at 31 March and vouching of a sample of March sales.

blocks.title: Strategy vs plan

concepts.title: Changes, supervision and documentation
body: The auditor updates the strategy and plan whenever unexpected events, changed conditions or evidence differ significantly from what was expected — e.g. tests of detail contradict tests of controls.
The nature, timing and extent of direction, supervision and review depend on the entity's size and complexity, the audit area, assessed risks, and the competence of individual team members.
Documentation: the overall strategy, the audit plan, and any significant changes with reasons. Standard programmes and checklists may be used if tailored to the engagement.
concepts.analogy: A plan in a drawer is useless; a plan updated and recorded is a map others can follow and check.
concepts.work: Peer reviewers check whether planning documents were updated when risks changed during the audit.

concepts.title: Audit programme: meaning and construction
body: An audit programme is a detailed, written list of examination and verification steps, arranged to show how they connect, designed with reference to the assertions in the financial statements — in effect a set of instructions for applying audit procedures.
One programme cannot fit all businesses because nature, size, controls and scope differ; the auditor frames a standard programme covering the essential minimum and adapts it with experience.

Assistants should keep an open mind and report significant matters beyond the programme to seniors. The programme must be reviewed periodically; working from an outdated programme may be treated as negligence.

Construction points: stay within the scope of the assignment; write the programme; identify the best available evidence; include only useful steps; state objectives and enough detail for each area; consider all possibilities of error; co-ordinate procedures for related items. Timing is usually flexible, except for things like observing stock counts or verifying cash and securities at year-end.
concepts.analogy: An audit programme is a recipe card for the team: ingredients (records), steps (procedures), quantities (sample sizes) — but a good cook still tastes as she goes.
concepts.work: Articled assistants sign off each step on the programme as they complete it.

concepts.title: Audit programme: evidence, merits and demerits
body: The programme is designed to obtain audit evidence. Broad sources of evidence: documents, physical examination, explanations of management and staff, third-party statements, the auditor's own calculations, internal controls, relationships among accounting data, subsidiary records, minutes, and subsequent actions.

Best evidence depends on the item: for cash in hand, a physical count; for investments pledged with a bank, the bank's certificate; for debtors, invoices, credit notes, statements and external confirmations taken together.
Merits and demerits are summarised in the table; the demerits are removed by periodic review, imaginative supervision and encouraging assistants to report unusual matters.
concepts.analogy: Evidence is like a jigsaw — no single piece shows the whole picture; the programme tells you which pieces to look for first.
concepts.work: A signed, updated audit programme is often the auditor's best defence in a negligence case.

Disadvantages (and remedy)

Work may become mechanical
Total view of the work in big audits
Programme may become rigid while the business changes
Easier allocation of work by ability
Weak assistants may hide behind "not in the programme"

illustrations.title: Sorting planning activities
illustrations.q: An auditor appointed for the first time by Godavari Auto Parts Ltd. does the following. Classify each as a preliminary engagement activity, part of the overall audit strategy, or part of the audit plan: (a) enquires about the integrity of the promoters; (b) checks the team's independence; (c) sends an engagement letter; (d) decides to use a valuation expert and to put senior staff on inventory at three plants; (e) fixes the reporting timetable with management; (f) decides to vouch a sample of 60 purchase invoices in December and March.

head: Activity
Classification
rows: (a) Integrity of promoters
Preliminary — acceptance/continuance of client
(b) Independence of team
Preliminary — compliance with ethical requirements
(c) Engagement letter
Preliminary — agreeing terms of engagement
(d) Expert and senior staff for inventory
Overall audit strategy — resources to deploy and where
(e) Reporting timetable
Overall audit strategy — reporting objectives and timing
(f) Sample of 60 invoices in Dec and Mar
Audit plan — nature, timing and extent of further procedures
solution.title: Answer

illustrations.title: A finance head writing the audit strategy
illustrations.q: The auditor of Tapi Textiles Ltd. asks the company's finance head to prepare the audit strategy and detailed procedures to save time, and adopts them unchanged. Comment.

solution.provision: SA 300 — the overall audit strategy and audit plan remain the auditor's responsibility
solution.facts: The auditor adopted a strategy and procedures written by the client's finance head.
solution.analysis: The auditor may discuss elements of planning with management, but care is needed not to compromise effectiveness; procedures known in advance lose their element of unpredictability and the client would effectively be auditing itself.
solution.conclusion: The approach is wrong — the auditor must establish the strategy and develop the plan himself.

jobs.title: Planning a first-year audit
jobs.situation: A new client manufactures auto parts at three plants with a large scrap business.
steps: Complete acceptance checks and communication with the previous auditor; send an engagement letter.
Set the strategy: reporting framework, deadlines, plants to visit, senior staff on inventory and scrap.
Write the plan and programme, including steps for scrap sales and stock — and update them when new risks appear.
jobs.takeaway: Strategy first, plan next, programme for the team — all living documents.

jobs.title: An assistant finds something not in the programme
jobs.situation: While matching sales invoices with e-way bills, many e-way bills are found cancelled within a day in March.
steps: Report it to the senior immediately — it may indicate fictitious year-end sales.
The senior updates the plan and programme for cut-off testing.
jobs.takeaway: The programme is a minimum, not a limit; report unusual matters.

mcqs.q: Which Standard on Auditing deals with planning an audit of financial statements?
mcqs.explain: SA 300 is the standard on planning an audit of financial statements so that the work is done effectively. SA 200 sets overall objectives, SA 230 covers documentation and SA 500 covers audit evidence. In practice: planning memos in audit files refer to SA 300 requirements.

mcqs.q: Audit planning is best described as:
options: A continuous and iterative process through the audit
A one-time step completed before fieldwork
An activity done only at year-end
A task delegated to the client
mcqs.explain: Planning often begins soon after the previous audit and continues until the current audit is completed; it is revised as new information arrives. It is not a discrete step or a client task. In practice: audit plans are updated after interim visits.

mcqs.q: Checking the integrity of a new client's promoters is part of:
mcqs.explain: Before planning, the auditor performs acceptance and continuance procedures, which include considering the integrity of principal owners and key management. The audit plan deals with procedures, not acceptance. In practice: firms decline clients whose promoters have a doubtful record.

mcqs.q: The overall audit strategy mainly determines the audit's:
options: Exact sample sizes for each account
mcqs.explain: The overall audit strategy decides the audit's scope, its timing and its direction, and guides the detailed audit plan. Sample sizes belong to the audit plan; accounting policies belong to management. In practice: strategy decides where experienced staff and experts are used.

mcqs.q: Deciding to involve a valuation expert for complex derivatives is part of:
mcqs.explain: The strategy determines which resources to deploy, including experts for complex matters. The engagement letter records terms, not resource decisions. In practice: deciding early on experts avoids delays and cost overruns near the reporting deadline.

mcqs.q: The audit plan includes:
options: Nature, timing and extent of risk assessment and further audit procedures
mcqs.explain: SA 300 requires the audit plan to describe what risk assessment and further audit procedures will be done, when and how much, plus any other procedures the SAs require. It is more detailed than the strategy. In practice: plans specify samples and dates.
mcqs.topic: The audit plan and its link with strategy

mcqs.q: Who is responsible for the overall audit strategy and audit plan?
mcqs.explain: The strategy and plan remain the auditor's responsibility; the auditor may discuss parts with management without compromising effectiveness. Letting the client prepare them would undermine independence and unpredictability. In practice: the engagement partner signs off the planning memo.
mcqs.topic: The audit plan and its link with strategy

mcqs.q: If tests of detail contradict the results of tests of controls, the auditor should:
options: Revise the strategy and plan and modify further procedures
Ask management to change the records
mcqs.explain: SA 300 requires the auditor to update the strategy and plan when evidence differs significantly from expectations, changing the nature, timing and extent of further procedures. Ignoring contradictory evidence would be negligent. In practice: reliance on controls may be withdrawn and substantive testing increased.

mcqs.q: The extent of supervision of engagement team members depends on all EXCEPT:
options: The size and complexity of the entity
The assessed risks of material misstatement
mcqs.explain: Supervision depends on entity size and complexity, the audit area, assessed risks and team members' capabilities. The fee does not determine how much supervision quality requires. In practice: high-risk areas handled by juniors get closer review.

mcqs.q: Which of these must be documented under SA 300?
options: Overall strategy, audit plan and significant changes with reasons
Only the fee and engagement letter
mcqs.explain: The auditor documents the overall audit strategy, the audit plan and significant changes to either with the reasons. This records key decisions, supports review by seniors and explains the final approach. In practice: tailored standard checklists are often used.

mcqs.q: An audit programme is:
options: A detailed written set of verification steps and instructions for the audit team
mcqs.explain: An audit programme lists the examination and verification steps, showing how they relate, with instructions on techniques and extent, so the team can gather evidence for the opinion. It is not the engagement letter or report. In practice: each step is signed by the person who performs it.

mcqs.q: Why is one standard audit programme for all businesses not practicable?
options: Businesses differ in nature, size, controls and scope of work
Programmes are not used in audits
mcqs.explain: Because nature, size, composition, controls and the scope of service vary, a single programme cannot suit all; a standard minimum programme is adapted to each client. Standard programmes are allowed if tailored. In practice: a bank audit programme differs greatly from a retailer's.

mcqs.q: For which of these does the auditor usually have no discretion over timing?
options: Observing the client's physical inventory count
mcqs.explain: Observation of stock-taking, and verification of cash and securities at year-end, must happen when the client counts or at the specific date. Other procedures can usually be scheduled flexibly. In practice: count dates are fixed in the strategy well in advance.

mcqs.q: The best evidence for cash in hand is:
mcqs.explain: Counting cash gives direct physical evidence of its existence; the cash book is the client's own record and representations are weak evidence. Bank statements relate to bank balances, not cash in hand. In practice: surprise cash counts are a common audit step.
mcqs.topic: Audit programme: evidence, merits and demerits

mcqs.q: A disadvantage of an audit programme is that:
options: Work may become mechanical and rigid
It is evidence of due care
mcqs.explain: The main drawbacks are mechanical work, rigidity, assistants hiding behind it and loss of initiative; fixing responsibility, guiding next year and evidencing due care are advantages. The drawbacks are cured by review and supervision. In practice: managers encourage assistants to question unusual items.
mcqs.topic: Audit programme: evidence, merits and demerits

mcqs.q: An assistant notices an unusual pattern not covered by the programme. He should:
options: Report it to his senior or partner
Ignore it since it is not in the programme
Discuss it only with client staff
mcqs.explain: Assistants should keep an open mind and report significant matters beyond the programme to seniors; the programme is a minimum, not a limit. Correcting the books is management's job. In practice: such reports often uncover cut-off manipulation or fraud.
mcqs.topic: Audit programme: evidence, merits and demerits

summary: SA 300: plan so the audit is effective.
Preliminary: acceptance/continuance, ethics and independence, terms of engagement.
Strategy = scope, timing, direction; plan = nature, timing, extent of procedures.
Update when evidence differs; document strategy, plan and changes with reasons.
Audit programme = detailed instructions; review periodically and supervise imaginatively.
remember: Strategy and plan remain the auditor's responsibility.
traps: Planning is not a one-time phase.
Sharing too much of the plan with management can reduce effectiveness.

viva.q: What are the three preliminary engagement activities?
viva.model: First, acceptance or continuance procedures for the client; second, checking that ethics and independence rules are met by the team; third, agreeing the terms of engagement with the client.

viva.q: What does the overall audit strategy set?
viva.model: It decides the audit's scope, its timing and its direction, and guides development of the detailed audit plan.

viva.q: What does SA 300 require the audit plan to describe?
viva.model: It describes what risk assessment procedures will be done, when and to what extent, the same for further audit procedures at the assertion level, and any other procedures the SAs require.

points.pt: Further audit procedures at assertion level

viva.q: What must be documented about planning?
viva.model: The strategy and the detailed plan, plus every significant change made to either during the engagement, with the reasons for it.

viva.q: How can the disadvantages of an audit programme be removed?
viva.model: By periodic review of the programme, imaginative supervision of assistants, and encouraging them to report significant matters even if not in the programme.

cases.title: First audit of Sabari Polymers Ltd.
cases.case: CA Neha accepts the first audit of Sabari Polymers Ltd. after enquiring about its promoters and checking her team's skills. She fixes the reporting deadline with management, decides to visit two of four plants and to engage a chemical engineer to assess stock quantities. Her office issues a detailed set of instructions to assistants. Mid-way, an assistant finds large scrap sales not recorded in the books; the instructions are silent on scrap.

mcqs.q: Enquiring about promoters and checking her team's skills are:
mcqs.explain: Considering the integrity of owners and the competence of the team are acceptance procedures, which are preliminary engagement activities before planning proper. They do not specify audit procedures, which belong to the plan. In practice: these are recorded in an acceptance checklist.

mcqs.q: Fixing the deadline, choosing plants to visit and engaging an engineer relate mainly to:
mcqs.explain: Reporting timetable, deployment of resources and use of experts are strategy matters that set scope, timing and direction. The programme gives detailed steps for assistants. In practice: these decisions are made early so the right resources are available.

mcqs.q: The detailed set of instructions issued to assistants is the:
mcqs.explain: A detailed, written list of verification steps and instructions for the team is the audit programme. The overall strategy is broader and does not list individual steps. In practice: assistants sign each completed step so responsibility can be traced.

mcqs.q: On learning about unrecorded scrap sales, CA Neha should:
options: Update the audit plan and programme to cover scrap
Ignore it as immaterial without assessment
mcqs.explain: SA 300 requires updating the strategy and plan when new information differs significantly from that used in planning; the programme must be revised to cover the risk. Continuing with outdated instructions could be negligent. In practice: scrap is a common area of revenue leakage.
